name: Uma Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a firm of six that does house electrics plus the newer stuff: car chargers on driveways, smart thermostats, door cameras, alarm systems. A typical day I'm in a suburb fitting a car charger with Priyanka, the owner, or on my own swapping out an old fuse box with her checking my photos. I'm the junior, still slow at the proper testing. But I'm the one everyone asks when the charger app won't connect to the house Wi-Fi.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the gadgets, honestly, and I like being the one who can explain them to a customer. What wears me out is that I'm a bit backwards: brilliant at the app, slow at the basics. Priyanka once watched me take twenty minutes to find a loose neutral she found in two. That stung.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh. That'd be a bit of a let-down. I use AI every day for planning jobs and writing up quotes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool, not a miracle, and that's fine. To my friends I'd say I told you it wasn't Skynet. At work I'd say we keep using it for quotes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job's in good shape. Every new car needs a charger on a driveway, and no amount of AI hype changes how many driveways there are. Callum, my boyfriend, drives a delivery van, and his job's fine in this one too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on my licence and push Priyanka to let me do more of the testing myself. I'd keep saving, around 200 a month, since we've got about five months put by. I'd keep using AI for the paperwork side because it saves me an hour a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty settled, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you use the AI for, exactly, on a typical job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before a charger job I give it the house details and photos and it drafts the cable route and the materials list. Then I check it against the rules and adjust. Priyanka was sceptical, but now she asks me to do it for her jobs too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're slow at the basics. Does using AI slow your learning of those?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, a bit. I lean on it for the thinking and then my hands are behind. I've started doing the fault-finding first without it, on purpose.

say: I'd say AI is a **useful tool**, not a miracle.
I'd tell friends it was **never Skynet**, and keep using it for quotes.
think: I think **car chargers** on driveways keep my job busy either way.
I think Callum's **delivery job** is fine here too.
do: Keep at my **licence** and do more testing myself.
Keep using **AI for paperwork**, saving an hour a day.
S0.quote: Every new car needs a charger on a driveway, and no amount of AI hype changes how many driveways there are.
fieldNote: Uma is **ahead on tech** but behind on basic electrical skills, and knows it.
She now **practises without AI** on purpose.
Her boss Priyanka has started **relying on her** AI drafts.

steps.text: Ask Priyanka to let her do more of the testing herself
Keep drafting charger cable routes and materials lists with AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the world I'm kind of expecting. The office stuff gets eaten, we get busier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the trades are a good place to be, and that young people should think about them. I'd say it online too, I post about my work sometimes. I'd say the firms that use AI well will win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm in a good spot for my job, but Callum's routes and dispatch go AI first, and that's a bit wobbly. My job is safe, but if the dispatch office goes to software, my boyfriend Callum gets his shifts planned by a machine that doesn't care about his bad back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build Priyanka a proper AI quoting and booking setup, so we can take more jobs. I'd ask for a pay rise once it's running. I'd do a smart-building course in the evenings, the systems that run lights and heating in offices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a bit uneasy about Callum. Excited about work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd ask for a pay rise. What if Priyanka said no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look around. A bigger firm that does building controls would want someone like me. But I'd rather stay, Priyanka taught me everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Callum change jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd hate to. He likes being on the road with his music. I'd nudge him toward a forklift ticket or something, but he'd do it in his own time.

say: I'd say the **trades** are a good place to be.
I'd say firms that use **AI well** will win.
think: I think **my job** is safe and busier.
I worry the depot's **dispatch software** will grind Callum down.
do: Build Priyanka an **AI quoting and booking** setup.
Ask for a **pay rise** once it's running.
feel: I feel **excited about work**, a bit uneasy about Callum.
S1.quote: My job is safe, but if the dispatch office goes to software, my boyfriend Callum gets his shifts planned by a machine that doesn't care about his bad back.
fieldNote: Uma's own job looks strong, but **Callum's work** is on her mind.
She'd turn her tech skill into a **pay rise** at the firm.
Her career path points to **building controls** in offices.

steps.text: Set up an AI quoting and booking system for Priyanka's firm
Take an evening course in smart building controls
Ask Priyanka for a pay rise once the system runs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for the thinking side, robots three years later. That's quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan, all of us, the government and firms. I'd say people who learn to work with the machines will be okay. I'd probably say it a bit too cheerfully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my quoting and app work goes first, in 2028, and that was my edge. The one thing I was better at than my boss, AI does by 2028, and my hands are still slower than hers. And Callum's van could be driving itself not long after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put everything into getting my hands as good as Priyanka's in two years: testing, fault-finding, every evening. I'd save hard, 400 a month, and put a bit into shares in robot and charger firms. I'd look for jobs fitting and servicing the robots themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd have a plan, but it'd be a race.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd invest in robot firms. How much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a thousand to start, out of our five months. Callum would think I'd lost it. But if robots take our jobs, I'd want a bit of the money they make.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Callum cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday in the spring, and probably the second car. We'd keep the flat because rent's fair and moving costs too much.

say: I'd say government and firms need **a plan** now.
I'd say people who **work with machines** will be okay.
think: I think my **quoting edge** goes to AI in 2028.
I fear my **hands** are still slower than my boss's.
do: Practise **testing and fault-finding** every evening for two years.
Save **400 a month** and buy some robot shares.
feel: I feel **anxious**, like it's a race.
S2.quote: The one thing I was better at than my boss, AI does by 2028, and my hands are still slower than hers.
fieldNote: Uma sees her **tech advantage** vanish first, which surprises her.
She'd **invest** a thousand in robot firms as a hedge.
Two household jobs at risk: hers later, **Callum's van** soon after.

steps.text: Practise testing and fault-finding every evening
Put 1,000 into shares in robot and charger companies
Apply for jobs servicing install robots
Drop the spring holiday and sell the second car

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots in 2034. Okay, that feels manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where it's worth getting skilled up now. I'd tell my mates in office jobs to start learning trades. I'd say the trades have a few good years ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have time to get properly good, and to move into building controls or robot servicing before 2034. With five years, I can stop being the girl who's good at apps and become an electrician who's good at everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my licence, then the smart-building course. I'd build up Priyanka's AI systems so the firm gets more work. I'd save 250 a month and talk to Callum about him training for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a forward way. Like a big job you're nervous about but ready for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Callum train for, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He likes fixing his bike. Maybe a bike or scooter mechanic, or maintenance for the delivery robots, ha. He'd decide, but I'd show him the courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay with Priyanka?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a few years, yes. After the licence, maybe I'd move to a firm doing big building systems. I'd tell her early, she'd understand.

say: I'd say it's worth getting **skilled up now**.
I'd tell office friends to **learn trades** while there's time.
I'd say the trades have **a few good years**.
think: I think there's time to move into **building controls** before 2034.
I want to be **good at everything**, not just apps.
do: Finish my **licence**, then the smart-building course.
Save **250 a month** and help Callum find a course.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, but nervous-ready, like before a big job.
S3.quote: With five years, I can stop being the girl who's good at apps and become an electrician who's good at everything.
fieldNote: Uma treats five years as **enough time** to fix her skill gap.
She'd likely **leave Priyanka** for building systems after the licence.
She'd steer **Callum** towards a course without pushing.

steps.text: Take the smart-building controls course after the licence
Expand the AI booking and quoting tools at Priyanka's firm
Show Callum mechanic and robot maintenance courses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots by 2039. That's loads of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news, honestly. I'd say it's exciting if you're young and like tech. I'd post about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be completely fine and maybe better off. Ten years is long enough for me to be the person who installs the robots instead of the person they replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do my licence, then move into building controls in four or five years. I'd set up a small side job helping older people with their smart-home gear at weekends. I'd keep using AI every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A side job for older people? Tell me more.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My nan can't work her thermostat. Half her street can't either. I'd charge 30 an hour to set up and explain the gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that makes you nervous in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only Callum, a bit, but ten years is time for him too. And whether I'd actually get good at the basics, but that's on me.

say: I'd say it's **good news**, honestly, and post about it.
I'd say it's **exciting** if you're young and like tech.
think: I think I'd be **completely fine**, maybe better off.
I'd be the one who **installs the robots**, not the one replaced.
do: Move into **building controls** in four or five years.
Start a weekend **smart-home help** service for older people.
feel: I feel **calm** and a bit excited.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough for me to be the person who installs the robots instead of the person they replace.
fieldNote: Uma sees a long warning as pure **opportunity**.
Her **side job** idea comes from her nan's thermostat.
Her only nerves are **Callum** and her own basic skills.

steps.text: Move into a building controls job within five years

Keep using AI daily for quotes and job planning

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my quoting edge goes in 2028 and Callum's van not long after. What would help is cheap evening courses for trades skills, and something for delivery drivers like Callum.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the gap between being good at tech and good at the trade. Everybody assumes the girl who's good with apps is the safe one, but my hands are what will keep me employed.

headlineQuote: Everybody assumes the girl who's good with apps is the safe one, but my hands are what will keep me employed.
portrait: Uma is a **27-year-old junior** fitting car chargers, smart-home kit and fuse boards.
She uses **AI every day** and is better with apps than with basic fault-finding.
She worries about **Callum**, her boyfriend, a delivery driver.
She'd **race to fix** her hands-on skills, and sees a long warning as opportunity.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, since her edge goes first and Callum's van follows.
